title: Northwest wildfires: Dangerous fire weather persists in as crews work to contain blazes | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Fire danger continues in the Pacific Northwest Saturday as flame-fueling winds reached their strongest point in days on Friday, challenging fire crews battling to keep destructive blazes from spreading in Spokane, Washington, across the region and into neighboring states, with at least three fire-related deaths reported.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson on Fridayannounced a public health emergencydeclared by the US Department of Health and Human Services in response to the devastating wildfires in the state.

Acomplex of three firesnear Spokane in the eastern portion of the state has scorched more than 10,000 acres of land and destroyed hundreds of homes and structures since igniting last Saturday. At one point, the fires forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate. Some have since returned to findtreasured memories turned to ashes.

The blazes – the Autumn Lane, Old Trails and Fairview fires – are being fought by California Team Seven, whose deputy incident commander, Nic Elmquist, described the response on arrival as tackling “a very complex, moving, rapidly expanding fire.”

The danger has spilled south into Nevada, too. The wind-driven Bug Fire has burned more than 4,000 acres north of Reno and continues to grow, forcing evacuations in the Cold Springs and Red Rock areas, where crews worked to protect homes, Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District Deputy Fire Chief Shannon Lewis said in a Saturdaylate-night briefing.

Crews from across the Tahoe basin joined the fight, with aircraft making drops through the night and a strike team dispatched to protect homes in the Red Rock area. “It’s been a very busy weekend for our firefighters,” Chief Lewis said, noting crews had battled two other fires the night before and worked through the night. “Our number one concern is life safety.”

Evacuation zones have expanded as the fire spreads. The main highway east of the Sierra Nevada stayed open, though officials closed one exit near the fire, according to theWashoe County Emergency Center.

In Reno, the Red Cross opened a shelter for evacuees and their animals. Those fleeing were urged to bring several days’ worth of essentials – medications, documents, phone chargers, food and water, a change of clothes – and to check the fire’s perimeter map for evacuation zones and road closures.

As the fight drags on, the toll on firefighters climbs. A dozer operator working on the Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon was fatally injured Thursday, and on Friday a helicopter on contract with the US Forest Service crashed while fighting the Widemouth 2 Fire in Utah, killing the pilot and one crew member,the National Interagency Fire Center announced.

The helicopter ignited vegetation in the surrounding area when it crashed and the site is now located inside the perimeter of the Widemouth 2 Fire, preventing emergency responders from accessing the victims, the fire center said in an update Saturday.

What caused the crash is under investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration, the fire center said.

Three firefighters have suffered burns, one seriously enough to be hospitalized twice and sent to a burn center. Elmquist added injuries tend to mount at this stage of a long fire, urging crews to “look out after each other.”

Meanwhile, crews have gained ground, shifting to the painstaking work of mopping up: hunting down and drowning the last pockets of heat behind the fire lines. By Friday, crews tackling the Fairview fire had pushed 150 to 200 feet inward from the perimeter in places, widening the ring of blackened, secured line. The most stubborn holdout was a recycling plant inside the fire, where crews kept water aimed at the site in what officials called a two- to three-day job.

Firefighters knocked down several new blazes Friday, and officials warned crews not to grow complacent during mop-up. Overnight operations into Saturday noted the fires did not move as the wind didn’t pick up, with crews focusing on mop-up efforts and patrolling.

More than 40 large fires are burning in Washington and Oregon — more than half of the nationwide total,according to the National Interagency Fire Center.It’s already theworst fire season in more than 30 yearsfor both states, one fueled by human-caused climate change. Smoke from these blazes is also tanking air quality in parts of the Northwest.

Authorities havearrested and chargeda Spokane resident with first-degree arson in one of the fires. The manadmittedto igniting the blaze and more than two dozen others since last year, court documents show.

Gusty winds persisted Saturday and, along with very dry conditions, maintained concerning fire weather.

A red flag warning is in effect for central and eastern Washington — including the Spokane area — and northern Oregon into at least Saturday night and may be extended. The warnings are issued by the National Weather Service to warn of weather conditions that may lead to dangerous wildfire spread.

Most areas of the Pacific Northwest and Intermountain West are seeing winds of 15 mph with gusts reaching 20 to 25 mph at times.

A similar ebb and flow of breezy winds is expected through at least early next week but the overall threat of fire spread will be less than Saturday’s.

High temperatures through the weekend and early next week will top out in the upper 80s to near 90 degrees, closer to normal summertime temperatures for the region and less intense than the heat fire crews had to contend with for much of the week.

Temperatures in Spokane, for example, are forecast to reach 92 degrees Saturday and are expected to reach 90 degrees on Sunday before returning to the 80s next week.

Stagnant smoke dropped air quality this week in the Pacific Northwest until winds Thursday and Friday cleared the worst of it from western locations, like Seattle and Portland, Oregon. But poor quality remains front and center for many east of the Cascades this weekend.

Smoke close to the surface — where it affects air quality the most — will also travel farther east on the same winds stoking the fire threat. Parts of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming will see their air quality degrade further this weekend.

Smoke higher in the atmosphere will also spread farther east into the Northern Plains and Midwest. This smoke is forecast to stay high enough that it is unlikely to cause a repeat of thewidespread smoky conditionsand poor air quality that affected many areas in the central and eastern US in July.

CNN’s Rebekah Riess contributed to this report.

CNN’s Rebekah Riess contributed to this report.
